title: FRM Valuation, Lesson 2: The binomial tree for option pricing
subtitle: The simplest model showing the whole logic - and the only one that can price an American option
whyItMatters: The binomial tree is where the no-arbitrage principle shows up most plainly, in simple arithmetic, and it handles what Black-Scholes cannot: the right to exercise early.
openingQuestion: In a one-step binomial model, how is the option price determined?
openingOptions: Build a portfolio of stock and borrowing that matches the option payoff on both branches
Take the probability-weighted average of the two future values and discount it at the stock's expected return
Multiply the current share price by the annual volatility
Take the market price of a similar listed option
explanation: The binomial tree prices an option by cutting time into steps, with only two possible price outcomes at each one. With two scenarios and two instruments - the stock and cash - there is always a portfolio that delivers exactly the option's value on both branches, and the cost of building that portfolio is the option price. What is striking is that the calculation never needs the true probability of either branch. Push the number of steps very high and the result converges to Black-Scholes.

diagram.label: Share price today, two scenarios at the next step
Compute delta: how many shares match the option value spread
Fund the remainder by borrowing or lending at the risk-free rate
Cost of the portfolio = the option price

realWorldExample.company: Why the binomial tree survives alongside a closed-form solution
realWorldExample.description: Black-Scholes gives an instant answer but only for European options - those exercisable strictly on the expiry date. An American option can be exercised at any time, and the value of that right depends on whether, at each node of the tree, exercising now beats holding on. The binomial tree can answer that question at every node; a closed-form solution has nowhere to ask it.

quiz.question: How is delta computed in a one-step binomial tree?
options: The option price divided by the current share price
The two future values averaged by true probability, then discounted
The option value spread across the two branches over the share price spread
Volatility multiplied by the square root of the time remaining
quiz.explanation: Delta is the number of shares needed for the portfolio to move in step with the option. Dividing the difference in option value by the difference in share price gives exactly that ratio - and it is the same delta that appears among the Greeks. Averaging by true probability is precisely what the no-arbitrage argument is built to avoid, dividing by the spot price yields a number with no hedging meaning, and volatility times the square root of time is a measure of dispersion rather than a hedge ratio.

quiz.question: Why does the binomial tree handle American options when Black-Scholes cannot?
options: Because Black-Scholes applies to commodities rather than equities
Because a tree uses a more accurate volatility than a closed form
Because American options have no expiry date at all
Because at each node you compare exercising now with holding on
quiz.explanation: Early exercise is a decision repeated at every moment, so valuing it requires a structure with intermediate points. The tree has nodes at which to ask the question at every step; a closed-form solution has only the expiry date. Black-Scholes applies to equities as readily as to anything else, it takes the same volatility input a tree does, and an American option certainly has an expiry - what it adds is the right to act before then.

quiz.question: As the number of steps in the tree grows very large, where does the result go?
options: It converges to the Black-Scholes formula price
It diverges as error accumulates through the steps
It reaches the option's intrinsic value today
It goes to 0 as each step's move gets smaller
quiz.explanation: This is the most elegant link in the chapter: as the number of steps goes to infinity, the binomial tree converges to the Black-Scholes price. The two models look very different but rest on the same underlying principle. Discretisation error shrinks rather than accumulating, intrinsic value ignores time value entirely, and the per-step move shrinks in a way that holds total volatility constant rather than driving the value to zero.

quiz.question: Why is the risk-neutral probability in a binomial tree not the market's true probability?
options: Because the true probability always exceeds the risk-neutral one for every asset
Because it is derived from the no-arbitrage condition, not from a forecast
Because true probabilities are unobservable, so a convention has to stand in
Because risk-neutral probability only works when the underlying pays no dividend
quiz.explanation: The whole pricing argument never needs to know how likely the stock is to rise. It only needs a portfolio that replicates the payoff in every scenario - and the cost of building that portfolio is the option price, whatever probabilities you personally believe. There is no general ordering between true and risk-neutral probabilities, dividends are handled by adjusting the tree rather than by invalidating the method, and the number is not a convention standing in for something unobservable: it is pinned down by the risk-free rate and the two branch levels.

quiz.question: Why can a binomial tree price an American option while the Black-Scholes formula cannot?
options: Because Black-Scholes applies only to assets paying a dividend
Because a tree needs no assumption at all about the return distribution
Because at each node you can compare exercising now with holding on
Because an American option is always exercised before its expiry date
quiz.explanation: Early exercise is a decision repeated at every moment, and the binomial tree already has the structure to test it at each node. A closed-form solution returns a single number with nowhere to insert that intermediate decision. Black-Scholes works on non-dividend-paying assets too, the tree does assume a specific two-state move at each step rather than being assumption-free, and an American option is frequently held to expiry - early exercise is a right, not an obligation.

practicePrompt.question: A one-step tree: the stock is at 100 and moves to either 120 or 90 after one period. A call option has a strike of 105. What is the option's delta?
options: 0.50 (= the 15 gap over the 30 gap)
0.15 (= 15 over the share price of 100)
1.00, because the option is already profitable
0.33 (= 10 divided by the gap of 30)
practicePrompt.explanation: On the up branch the option is worth 120 − 105 = 15; on the down branch it is worthless. Delta is the option value spread divided by the share price spread: 15 / (120 − 90) = 0.50. That number has a very concrete meaning - holding half a share for each option sold builds a replicating portfolio with the same cash flow on both branches, and the cost of building that portfolio IS the option price. Nowhere in the calculation does the true probability of a rise or a fall appear, and that is the whole power of the no-arbitrage principle.

keyTakeaways: Option price = cost of the replicating portfolio, with no true probability required
Delta = the option value spread divided by the share price spread
The tree handles American options because each node lets you compare exercising with holding
As the number of steps goes to infinity, the tree converges to the Black-Scholes price

summary.keyIdea: The binomial tree is the no-arbitrage principle written out in school arithmetic, and the standard tool for any option carrying an early exercise right
summary.commonMistake: Using the true up and down probabilities instead of the risk-neutral ones when rolling back through the nodes
summary.action: When you meet a complicated option, ask first whether it carries an early exercise right - if it does, you need a tree

application.title: Build a one-step tree yourself
application.message: Stock at 100, moving to either 120 or 80 after one period. A call struck at 100 is worth either 20 or 0. Delta = (20−0)/(120−80) = 0.5 - that is, half a share plus a loan replicates the option.
application.secondary: Do it by hand once and the entire option pricing chapter opens up.

sections.text: The binomial tree is taught before Black-Scholes not because it matters less, but because it is the only place where you can see the whole argument in addition and subtraction.

Over one step the share price can only go up or down. We have two instruments with which to replicate: the stock itself and cash at the risk-free rate. Two equations, two unknowns - always solvable. The number of shares required is delta.

variables.name: Option value on the up branch and the down branch
Share price on the up branch and the down branch

sections.text: For an American option, at each node we compare two numbers: the value of exercising right there, and the value of holding on. Take the larger and roll back toward the root. The node structure is what makes that comparison possible - and the reason a closed-form solution is helpless.

sections.label: Risk-neutral probability, not true probability
sections.text: When rolling back through the tree, the weights applied to the two branches are risk-neutral probabilities - quantities derived from the risk-free rate and the size of the two branches, not from anyone's belief about whether the stock will rise.
Two steps, and the numbers appear

Keep the numbers from the previous lesson: price 100, each step up 20% or down 10%, risk-free rate 5% per period, so the risk-neutral probability remains π = 0.5. After two steps the price can be 144, 108 or 81. A call struck at 100 pays 44, 8 and 0 respectively. Roll back node by node: on the upper branch the value is (0.5×44 + 0.5×8)/1.05 = 24.76; on the lower branch, (0.5×8 + 0.5×0)/1.05 = 3.81. One more step back to the root: (0.5×24.76 + 0.5×3.81)/1.05 = 13.61. The entire method is one calculation repeated from right to left.
What the closed form cannot do

The tree becomes essential once the option allows early exercise. Take a PUT struck at 100 on the same tree. At the node where the price is 90 after step one, the value of holding on is (0.5×0 + 0.5×19)/1.05 = 9.05. But exercising right there collects 100 − 90 = 10. With an American option the holder takes the 10 - and that 10 is what gets carried back toward the root in place of 9.05.

sections.label: The 0.45 gap is exactly the early exercise right
sections.text: Roll it all the way back: the European put prices at 4.31, the American put at 4.76. The 0.45 difference is the price of being able to choose the moment - something Black-Scholes cannot value, because it assumes exercise only at expiry. This is the practical reason the binomial tree was never displaced by the closed form: every contract with an American-style option, a call provision, or any decision taken part-way along needs a step-by-step model. And the condition for it to run correctly is a single one - at every node, compare the value of holding on with the value of exercising now, and take the larger.

lines: A tree with two branches contains the whole idea of modern derivatives pricing.
Next lesson: what happens when the number of steps goes to infinity.
